_about: The interactive comparative (#compare in english.html): one theme, answered as a 30 + 40 question. For each theme: best, the text that stands best on its own in part (a), and why; points, for each text, the points to choose from for part (a) (moments m are key moment numbers, 1 to 12); links, the strong links between two texts' key moments for part (b) (rel: same, differ or degree; say: a model comparison sentence); ends, for each pair of texts, the judgement to end part (b) on. A pair of moments is a link only if it is listed; build_eng.py checks every moment and pair.

themes.name: Abuse of power
themes.what: Who has power, how they use it to control or hurt people, who suffers, and whether anyone stands up to them.
themes.bestWhy: Shawshank shows abuse of power most openly, so it stands on its own in part (a). Sive and Small Things Like These are both set in a controlling small Irish community, so they compare best together in part (b).

shawshank.title: Power through fear and violence
shawshank.say: Norton greets the new men with “discipline and the Bible”, and that night Hadley beats a frightened prisoner to death. Nobody holds him to account.

shawshank.title: Power over the mind
shawshank.say: Fifty years of control leave Brooks unable to live outside, and he hangs himself. Even Red, once freed, asks permission to go to the toilet.

shawshank.title: Killing to keep control
shawshank.say: When Tommy could prove Andy innocent, Norton has him shot, because Andy is too useful at hiding the warden's money.

shawshank.title: Power turned back on the powerful
shawshank.say: Andy uses brains, not force: tax advice wins beer for the crew, and the false name Andy made up to hide the warden's money is what brings the warden down.

sive.title: Money decides everything
sive.say: Once Thomasheen offers £200, it is Mena who drives the match and works on Mike until he gives in. A girl's life has a price.

sive.title: The powerless have no say
sive.say: Sive's schooling, her bed and her marriage are all decided for her. Mena announces each decision; she never asks.

sive.title: Lies and burned words
sive.say: Mena lies that Liam has left Sive for good, and Thomasheen burns Liam's letter, so Sive never learns there was a way out.

sive.title: Bullying the weak into silence
sive.say: When Nanna stands up for Sive, Mena and Thomasheen threaten to send her to the county home.

stlt.title: Quiet, polite control
stlt.say: The Mother Superior controls every minute of Bill's visit: Sarah washed and dressed, the night in the shed called a game, and a hint that school places are scarce.

stlt.title: Locked doors
stlt.say: The girls are kept behind walls topped with broken glass; one begs to be taken to the river, and Sarah is locked all night in the freezing coal shed.

stlt.title: Fear keeps the town quiet
stlt.say: Eileen says there are things you have to ignore, and Mrs Kehoe warns that the nuns have “a finger in every pie”. Their power depends on everyone's silence.

stlt.title: One man stands up to it
stlt.say: Bill goes back for Sarah and walks her through the town, knowing he will pay for it. Power can be broken, but at a cost.

links.say: In both texts money is the tool of power: just as the £200 buys Sive's future, the Mother Superior's envelope of money is meant to buy Bill's silence.
In both texts a woman carries out the abuse for a system bigger than her: Mena announces every decision about Sive, and the Mother Superior smoothly protects the convent's secrets.
Like Sive, who is told she will leave school and marry an old man, Sarah has no say at all: she is locked in a coal shed and her baby is taken from her.
In both texts escape is cut off: Thomasheen burns the letter that would have freed Sive, and the convent girls are kept behind walls topped with broken glass.
In both texts abuse goes on because decent people look away: Mike cannot look his mother in the face, and Eileen tells Bill there are things you have to ignore.
Fear silences anyone who might object: Nanna is threatened with the county home, and Mrs Kehoe warns Bill that the nuns have a finger in every pie.
Here the texts part ways: in Sive nobody stops the abuse and Sive dies in the bog, whereas in Small Things Like These Bill walks back to the convent and takes Sarah out.
Both endings are touched by the abuse, but Small Things Like These is far more hopeful: Sive ends in grief with the powerful unpunished, while Bill walks home happy, though he knows he will pay.
Greed is at the root of both: Mena pushes the match for the £200, and Norton has Tommy killed to protect the money Andy hides for him.
Both abusers destroy the truth to keep control, but Norton goes much further: Thomasheen burns a letter, while Norton has a witness shot dead.
Both texts show the strong bullying the weak, but Shawshank is far more brutal: Nanna is threatened with the county home, while Hadley beats a frightened man to death.
The weapons are different: in Sive power works through money and words, whereas in Shawshank it works through fists, guns and solitary confinement.
In both texts the abuse of power drives a powerless person to death: Sive drowns in the bog, and Brooks, broken by fifty years of control, hangs himself.
Nanna pleads with Mike and fails, whereas Andy outwits the warden completely: in Sive the powerless lose, in Shawshank one of them wins.
The endings could not be more different: Sive closes on a lament over her body, while Shawshank closes on two free men on a sunlit beach.
In both texts the abuser hides behind religion: Norton talks of discipline and the Bible, and the Mother Superior covers cruelty with politeness and a Christmas card.
Both texts punish people by shutting them away: Andy gets two weeks in solitary for playing music, and Sarah is locked all night in the freezing coal shed.
Both hide the truth to protect themselves, but Norton is far more violent: the Mother Superior calls the night in the shed a game, while Norton has Tommy shot.
In both texts power gets inside people's heads: Brooks can no longer live without the prison, and the town has learnt there are things you have to ignore.

links.aspect: No one is held to account
links.say: In both worlds the powerful answer to no one: nobody holds Hadley to account for killing a prisoner, and Mrs Kehoe warns that the nuns have a finger in every pie.
Both texts show one man standing up to power, but Andy's victory is total, while Bill's quiet act of courage leaves him facing a cost we never see.
Both end in hope, but Shawshank's is complete, two free men on a beach, while Small Things Like These stops at Bill's door, before we see the price.

ends.sive|stlt: Power wins completely in Sive: Sive dies and the powerful go unpunished. In Small Things Like These one decent man breaks the silence, so its view of power is darker in what it shows but more hopeful in how it ends.
ends.shawshank|sive: Sive shows power winning; Shawshank shows it beaten. The same abuse that destroys Sive is finally turned back on Norton, so Shawshank leaves us far more hopeful.
ends.shawshank|stlt: Both texts show one man standing up to an abusive system, but Shawshank's victory is complete, while Small Things Like These ends in a quieter, more uncertain hope.

reps.title: The system's power over an innocent man
reps.say: Andy is convicted of two murders he didn't commit: a cold court decides his whole life in one verdict.
reps.start: From the opening scene, the film makes clear how much power the system holds over one man's life:
ideas: One verdict takes away the rest of a man's life, and the system never questions itself.
It sets up the whole film: power does not care whether you are guilty or innocent.
model: From the film's opening minutes, Darabont makes clear that the system holds total power over one man's life, whether he is guilty or not.
We first meet Andy Dufresne drunk in his car outside the house where his wife is with her lover, loading a revolver, and soon he is convicted of both murders and given two life sentences.
Darabont cross-cuts between that night and the courtroom, so we, like the jury, piece together a story that looks damning yet proves nothing.
This cold, impersonal verdict establishes the injustice at the heart of the film: once the system has decided, an innocent man is powerless to fight back.

words: evidence that only hints at guilt; it does not prove it
with no way to fight back
details: Andy sits drunk in his car outside the house where his wife is with her lover, loading a revolver.
At the trial he insists he threw the gun into the river.
He is given two life sentences for two murders he did not commit.

techniques.name: Cross-cutting
techniques.say: Darabont cross-cuts between Andy drunk in his car and the courtroom, so we judge him in pieces, just as the jury does.
techniques.what: Jumping back and forth between two scenes.

techniques.name: Music against the image
techniques.say: A soft old love song plays on Andy’s car radio as he loads the gun, a chilling contrast with what seems to be happening.
techniques.what: Music that clashes with what we see, to unsettle us.

reps.title: The system decides who is free
reps.say: After twenty years, Red's freedom depends on a few men behind a table, and one stamp, REJECTED, ends his hope.
reps.start: Power over the prisoners' futures lies entirely with the parole board:
ideas: The board holds all the power, and Red's future comes down to a stamp.
Freedom is not earned here: it is handed out, or not, by men who barely look up.
model: The parole board embodies the arbitrary authority the system holds over every prisoner's future.
Twenty years into his sentence, Red sits before the board and assures them he is a changed man, only for his file to be stamped 'REJECTED'.
Darabont cuts to a close-up of the stamp coming down, so that twenty years of a man's life are dismissed in a single word.
Freedom here is not earned but handed out, or withheld, by men who barely look up, which underlines how little control the prisoners have over their own lives.

reps.title: Power makes people perform
reps.say: Red says what he thinks the board wants to hear: under that kind of power, honesty seems pointless.
reps.start: Under the board's power, even Red's words are not his own:
ideas: Power makes honesty pointless: Red says what they want to hear, and it still isn't enough.
The system turns men into performers.
model: Under the board's power, even Red's words are not his own.
In a rehearsed and hollow speech, he tells the board exactly what he thinks they want to hear: that he has learned his lesson, that he is a changed man and no longer a danger to society.
The close-up of the 'REJECTED' stamp that follows exposes how futile the performance is.
The system demands that prisoners act out their remorse, yet it is unmoved even when they do, so honesty and dignity become the first casualties of its authority.

words: decided on a whim, not for good reasons
the right to give orders and decide
done the same way every time, without care
treating people as less than human
accepting something bad because you can't change it
details: Twenty years into a life sentence, Red tells the parole board he is a changed man.
His file is stamped REJECTED.
In voiceover he introduces himself as the prisoner who can get things smuggled in.

techniques.name: Close-up
techniques.say: A close-up of the stamp coming down on his papers, REJECTED, sums up twenty years in a single word.
techniques.what: A shot from very near, so one detail fills the screen.

techniques.name: Voiceover
techniques.say: Red’s calm voiceover takes over at once, introducing himself as the man who can get things, as if the board’s answer barely touches him.
techniques.what: A character’s voice speaking over the pictures.

reps.title: Power through fear and violence
reps.say: On Andy's first night Hadley beats a frightened prisoner to death, and nobody holds him to account.
reps.start: From the first night, Shawshank is ruled by fear:
ideas: The guards can kill a man for crying, and nothing happens to them.
Fear is the first lesson Shawshank teaches.
model: From Andy's first night, Shawshank is ruled by fear, and the guards wield their power with complete impunity.

When a terrified new prisoner, mockingly nicknamed 'Fat Ass' by Heywood, breaks down in tears, Captain Hadley beats him so savagely that he dies in the infirmary; the next morning, Andy is the only one who asks what his name was.
Darabont films that night in near-darkness, with the men behind bars, so the prison feels less like an institution than a cage.
The brutality is chilling precisely because nobody is held to account: a man can be killed for crying, and the regime carries on as normal. Fear is the first lesson Shawshank teaches.

reps.title: Religion as a mask
reps.say: Norton greets the new men with “discipline and the Bible” while he runs a brutal prison.
reps.start: Norton hides his cruelty behind religion:
ideas: Norton uses the Bible to look holy while his prison runs on violence.
The film warns us not to trust power that dresses itself up as goodness.
model: Norton hides the cruelty of his regime behind a mask of religion.
Greeting the new prisoners, he tells them he believes in two things, discipline and the Bible, and that here they will receive both.
Norton's own dialogue sets up his hypocrisy from his very first scene: scripture, for him, is less a source of mercy than a tool of control.
Within hours, Hadley has beaten a frightened man to death, and the warden's talk of righteousness rings hollow. Darabont warns us not to trust power that dresses itself up as goodness.

words: saying one thing and doing the opposite
reveals something bad that was hidden
details: Norton tells the new men he believes in discipline and the Bible.
That night Heywood and others taunt the new arrivals until one breaks down crying.
Hadley beats the crying man, who dies in the infirmary; the next morning Andy asks what his name was.

techniques.name: Aerial shot
techniques.say: As the bus arrives, a sweeping aerial shot takes in the prison’s huge stone walls, and the new men look tiny beside them.
techniques.what: A shot from high above: the place looks huge and the people small.

techniques.name: Lighting
techniques.say: The first night is filmed in near-darkness, with the men behind bars, so the prison feels like a cage.
techniques.what: How light and dark are used to set a mood.

techniques.name: Dialogue
techniques.say: Norton’s own words, “discipline and the Bible”, set up his hypocrisy from his very first scene.
techniques.what: What characters say, and how it reveals them.

reps.title: Knowledge is a quieter kind of power
reps.say: By offering tax advice, Andy turns Hadley from a threat into a favour: brains beat brute force.
reps.start: Andy discovers that knowledge can be as powerful as force:
ideas: Andy's knowledge gives him a power the guards don't have.
For a moment the prisoners hold the power, and Red says they felt like free men.
model: Andy discovers that knowledge can be as powerful as force.

While tarring the roof of the licence-plate factory, he overhears Hadley complaining about tax on an inheritance and dares to offer advice; Hadley nearly throws him off the roof, but within minutes Andy has explained how to keep the money tax-free, asking only for three beers each for his co-workers.
Red's voiceover puts the moment into words: the men sat and drank with the sun on their shoulders and felt like free men.
In a striking reversal, the brutal guard ends up serving the prisoners, which suggests that brains, not brute force, are the one weapon the powerless can turn against the powerful.

reps.title: Using power for others
reps.say: Andy asks only for beers for his crew: unlike the guards, he uses his power to give, not to take.
reps.start: Unlike the guards, Andy uses what power he has for others:
ideas: Andy uses his small win for others, not himself: the opposite of the guards.
Power used kindly is rare, and precious, in Shawshank.
model: Unlike the guards, Andy uses what little power he has for others rather than himself.
Having won Hadley over with his tax advice, he asks for nothing for himself except three beers each for his co-workers.
Darabont frames Andy sitting apart from the drinking men, smiling, as warm sunlight falls across the rooftop.
The contrast with the guards could not be sharper: where they use their authority to take, Andy uses his to give, and his small act of dignity hints at a different, more humane kind of strength.

words: an advantage you can use to get what you want
clever and good at judging people
details: The prisoners are tarring the roof of the licence-plate factory.
Hadley nearly throws Andy off the roof for daring to speak to him.
Andy explains how to keep the inheritance tax-free and asks only for three beers each for his co-workers.

techniques.name: Lighting and colour
techniques.say: The rooftop is bathed in warm sunlight, the opposite of the grey yard below.
techniques.what: How light and colour set a mood.

techniques.name: Voiceover
techniques.say: Red’s voiceover puts the moment into words: they sat and drank with the sun on their shoulders and felt like free men.
techniques.what: A character’s voice speaking over the pictures.

techniques.name: Framing
techniques.say: Andy sits apart from the others, smiling: the man who made it happen asks nothing for himself.
techniques.what: Where a character is placed in the shot, and what that says.

reps.title: Power over the mind
reps.say: Fifty years of control leave Brooks unable to live outside: the prison has taken over his mind.
reps.start: The prison's power reaches beyond its walls and into the mind:
ideas: The prison's power does not end at the gate: it has taken over his mind.
Fifty years of control have left Brooks unable to live without it.
model: The prison's power reaches far beyond its walls and into the minds of the men inside.
When Brooks Hatlen learns he is to be paroled after fifty years, he holds a knife to Heywood's throat in the hope of being kept inside, and Red explains that he is 'institutionalized'.
Once Brooks is released, a montage of rushing cars and busy streets makes the outside world seem fast and frightening to a man conditioned by half a century of routine.
The tragedy is that the system has made Brooks dependent on the very thing that imprisoned him; Shawshank has stripped him of the ability to live as a free man.

reps.title: The human cost of power
reps.say: Freed but broken, Brooks hangs himself after carving “Brooks Hatlen was here”.
reps.start: The cost of the prison's power is measured in a human life:
ideas: The system takes a man's whole life and gives nothing back.
Brooks's death is the true cost of power without limits.
model: The true cost of the prison's power is measured in a human life.
Freed but broken, Brooks cannot cope with the changed world, and he hangs himself in his halfway-house room after carving 'Brooks Hatlen was here' into a wooden beam.
Darabont's camera lingers on those carved words, a poignant final attempt to prove that he existed at all.
This haunting moment underscores how completely the system takes a man's life and gives nothing back: unchecked power does not simply punish, it destroys.

words: so used to an institution that you can't live without it
trained to think or act a certain way
details: Told he will be paroled after fifty years, Brooks holds a knife to Heywood's throat so he can stay inside.
Red explains that Brooks is 'institutionalized'.
Outside, Brooks cannot cope, and he hangs himself after carving 'Brooks Hatlen was here'.

techniques.name: Voiceover from a letter
techniques.say: Brooks’s letter to the men is read in his own voice over pictures of the outside world, so we hear his loneliness.
techniques.what: A character’s voice speaking over the pictures.

techniques.name: Montage
techniques.say: A rush of cars and busy streets makes the outside world look fast and frightening to a man who has been inside for fifty years.
techniques.what: A run of quick shots that sums up a time or a feeling.

techniques.name: Close-up
techniques.say: The camera lingers on the words he carves, “Brooks Hatlen was here”, before his death.
techniques.what: A shot from very near, so one detail fills the screen.

reps.title: Punished for a moment of freedom
reps.say: Andy gets two weeks in solitary for playing music: the guards can't stand anything they don't control.
reps.start: Even a moment of beauty is treated as a threat:
ideas: The guards punish beauty because it is something they don't control.
Even a few minutes of freedom is treated as a crime.
model: In Shawshank, even a moment of beauty is treated as a threat to the warden's control.

Andy locks himself in the office and plays a duet from Mozart's The Marriage of Figaro over the loudspeakers; across the yard, the prisoners stand frozen, listening, and Andy is punished with two weeks in solitary.
Because the opera comes through the prison's own loudspeakers, every man in the yard hears it: for a few minutes, the instrument of control becomes an instrument of liberation.
The punitive response exposes how the regime fears anything it cannot command, even a song.

reps.title: Power can't reach the inside
reps.say: Andy says music is something inside that they can't take from you: control has its limits.
reps.start: This scene suggests there is something power can never reach:
ideas: Andy says music is something inside that they can't take from you.
Power can lock up the body, but not everything inside a person.
model: This scene suggests there is something that power can never reach.
After two weeks in solitary, Andy tells the other men that music is something inside you that they can't take from you, while Red warns that hope is a dangerous thing.
Red's voiceover admits he has no idea what those two Italian ladies were singing about, yet for a brief moment every man in Shawshank felt free.
However tightly the warden controls their bodies, he cannot control their inner lives, and that resilience is the first sign that the prison's power has limits.

details: Andy's letters finally win books and records for the library.
He locks himself in the office and plays Mozart over the loudspeakers.
The prisoners stand still in the yard to listen, and Andy is given two weeks in solitary.

techniques.name: Music in the scene
techniques.say: The opera plays over the prison’s own loudspeakers, so every man in the yard hears it: the music is part of the story, not just the soundtrack.
techniques.what: Diegetic sound: music or noise the characters can hear too.

techniques.name: Wide shot
techniques.say: The camera rises over the yard as the men stand frozen, looking up, as if the music has stopped time.
techniques.what: A shot from far away, taking in the whole scene.

techniques.name: Voiceover
techniques.say: Red admits he has no idea what the singers were singing about, yet for a moment every man in Shawshank felt free.
techniques.what: A character’s voice speaking over the pictures.

reps.title: Killing to keep control
reps.say: Norton has Tommy shot so that Andy, who hides his illegal money, can never leave.
reps.start: Norton's power is so absolute that he will kill to protect it:
ideas: Norton would rather kill an innocent young man than lose the man who hides his money.
Power at the top of Shawshank answers to no one.
model: Norton's power is so absolute that he will kill to protect it.
When Tommy reveals that a former cellmate boasted of the murders Andy was convicted of, Norton refuses to help, throws Andy into solitary, and has Hadley shoot Tommy dead.
Darabont stages the killing at night, out in the dark yard, where the warden's crime can be hidden from everyone.
Norton would rather murder an innocent young man than lose the prisoner who hides his money, a ruthless act that reveals how the abuse of power protects itself at any cost.

reps.title: Corruption at the top
reps.say: The man who preaches the Bible is hiding stolen money and having a witness murdered.
reps.start: Corruption runs from the very top of Shawshank:
ideas: The man who quotes the Bible is the most corrupt man in the prison.
Corruption is not a few bad guards: it runs from the warden down.
model: Corruption at Shawshank runs from the very top.
Norton, who greeted the new men with talk of the Bible, has been using Andy to hide his illegal profits for years, and when Tommy's evidence threatens that arrangement, he silences him for good.
Andy's furious cry, 'How can you be so obtuse?', is laced with irony: Norton understands perfectly, and that is exactly why he will not help.
The most self-serving man in Shawshank is the one who preaches morality, and Darabont exposes the hypocrisy that lets corruption flourish unchecked.

words: willing to do anything, without pity
dishonest use of power for your own gain
using someone unfairly for your own benefit
frightening in a cold, quiet way
using power wrongly to hurt others
details: Tommy reveals that a former cellmate boasted of the murders Andy was convicted of.
Norton refuses to help and throws Andy into solitary when he protests.
Norton has Hadley shoot Tommy dead at night, and threatens to destroy the library.

techniques.name: Darkness
techniques.say: Tommy is shot at night, out in the dark yard, where no one can see what is done to him.
techniques.what: How light and dark are used to set a mood.

techniques.name: Dialogue
techniques.say: Andy’s angry cry, “How can you be so obtuse?”, marks the moment his patience snaps, and it gets him locked away.
techniques.what: What characters say, and how it reveals them.

reps.title: Hope as a way of resisting
reps.say: After Tommy's death, Andy tells Red to “get busy living”: choosing hope is his answer to Norton's power.
reps.start: Faced with Norton's power, Andy chooses hope:
ideas: Hope becomes Andy's way of fighting back.
Choosing to 'get busy living' is a quiet refusal to let Norton win.
model: Faced with the full weight of Norton's power, Andy chooses hope as his act of resistance.
After Tommy's death, he tells Red about his dream of a small hotel in Zihuatanejo and sums up the choice facing every prisoner: 'Get busy living, or get busy dying.'
Darabont films the two men side by side against the wall, close enough that every pause carries weight.
Choosing to keep living is a quiet refusal to let the system break him; the warden can control his days, but not his determination.

reps.title: What power does to people
reps.say: When Red hears Andy has asked for a rope, he fears the worst: power has pushed Andy to the edge.
reps.start: The scene also reveals how close Norton's power has pushed Andy to breaking:
ideas: Norton's power has pushed Andy to the edge.
The tension lets us feel how close power comes to breaking him.
model: The scene also reveals how close Norton's power has pushed Andy to breaking point.
Andy admits he drove his wife away, though he did not kill her, and makes Red promise to look under a rock near Buxton; when Red learns Andy has asked for a length of rope, he fears the worst.
Red's anxious voiceover builds suspense, leaving us, like him, unsure whether Andy plans to escape or to die.
The ambiguity is unsettling: years of abuse have left even the most resilient man on the edge, a bleak reminder of the human toll of unchecked authority.

words: the ability to survive something hard
gets a feeling or idea across
could mean more than one thing
details: Andy admits he was a distant husband, though he did not kill his wife.
He tells Red about his dream of a small hotel in Zihuatanejo, Mexico.
He makes Red promise to look under a rock near Buxton, and Red fears Andy plans to kill himself.

techniques.name: Two-shot
techniques.say: The two men sit side by side against the wall, filmed close, so every pause carries weight.
techniques.what: Two characters together in one shot, so we watch them react to each other.

techniques.name: Voiceover and suspense
techniques.say: Red’s voiceover tells us Andy has asked for a length of rope, and the fear of what he means to do builds suspense.
techniques.what: Holding back what happens next, so we worry.

reps.title: Power outwitted
reps.say: Behind a poster, Andy has spent nearly twenty years digging his way out: the warden's total control was never total.
reps.start: The empty cell reveals that the warden's control was never as complete as it seemed:
ideas: The warden's total control was an illusion all along.
The powerless man beats the system with time and patience.
model: The empty cell reveals that the warden's control was never as complete as it seemed.
At the morning count, Andy is gone; in a rage, Norton hurls a stone at the poster on the wall, and it tears straight through to a tunnel.
Darabont's reveal turns on a single shot: the stone vanishing into the hole exposes twenty years of secret, patient work behind the warden's back.
The irony is complete: the man Norton thought he owned had been outwitting him all along, and the system's power proves to be an illusion.

reps.title: Freedom through patience
reps.say: Andy crawls through five hundred yards of sewer pipe and raises his arms in the rain.
reps.start: Andy's escape is the reward for years of patient resistance:
ideas: Freedom comes from years of quiet, stubborn hope.
Andy raising his arms in the rain feels like a rebirth.
model: Andy's escape is the reward for years of patient, quiet resistance.
A flashback reveals that he dug through the wall for nearly twenty years with a small rock hammer, then crawled through five hundred yards of sewer pipe to freedom.
Darabont ends the sequence with Andy standing in the pouring rain, arms raised and lit by lightning, an image of rebirth.
Liberation here is earned by ingenuity rather than force, which suggests that the most enduring answer to abuse of power is a hope that refuses to die.

words: to beat someone by being cleverer
calmly waiting for a long time
when things turn out the opposite of what you'd expect
a new start, like being born again
details: At the morning count, Andy's cell is empty.
Norton throws a stone at the poster and it tears straight through to a tunnel.
Andy dug for nearly twenty years with a small rock hammer and crawled through five hundred yards of sewer pipe.

techniques.name: The reveal
techniques.say: The stone Norton throws tears straight through the poster: one shot reveals twenty years of secret work.
techniques.what: A shot that suddenly lets us see what was hidden.

techniques.name: Flashback
techniques.say: A flashback, narrated by Red, takes us back through the escape step by step.
techniques.what: Going back in time to see what happened earlier.

techniques.name: Weather and lighting
techniques.say: Andy stands in the pouring rain with his arms raised, lit by lightning, like a man being reborn.
techniques.what: Using weather and light to say something about a character.

reps.title: Power turned back on the powerful
reps.say: Andy uses the false name he invented to hide Norton's money to take that money and expose him.
reps.start: In the end, the system Norton built is the one that destroys him:
ideas: The system Norton built to hide his crimes is what destroys him.
Power turned back on its owner feels like justice.
model: In the end, the system Norton built to protect himself is what destroys him.
Posing as 'Randall Stephens', the false identity he created to hide the warden's money, Andy withdraws it from bank after bank and posts the account book to a newspaper.
A brisk montage of Andy, smartly dressed, moving from one counter to the next makes the warden's downfall feel unstoppable.
There is poetic justice in this reversal: the corruption Norton relied on becomes the weapon that brings him down, and the powerless man walks away free.

reps.title: Hypocrisy exposed
reps.say: Norton's safe is hidden behind the words “His judgment cometh and that right early”, and judgement does come.
reps.start: Norton's hypocrisy is finally exposed:
ideas: Behind “His judgment cometh” sits a safe full of dirty money.
The hypocrite is finally judged by his own words.
model: As the police arrive, he opens his safe, hidden behind the embroidered words 'His judgment cometh and that right early', to find Andy's Bible, its pages cut out to hold the rock hammer; moments later, he shoots himself.
The camera lingers on the embroidered verse, so the warden's end feels like judgement arriving at last.
The book Norton used as a symbol of discipline literally hid the means of escape, an irony that lays bare how hollow his piety always was.

when things turn out the opposite of what you'd expect
saying one thing and doing the opposite
giving a sense that things are right
details: Posing as 'Randall Stephens', Andy withdraws Norton's money from several banks.
He posts the warden's account book and evidence of his crimes to a newspaper.
Hadley is arrested; Norton finds the Bible that hid the rock hammer, and shoots himself.

techniques.name: Montage
techniques.say: A quick montage of Andy at bank after bank, smartly dressed, makes the warden’s downfall feel unstoppable.
techniques.what: A run of quick shots that sums up a time or a feeling.

techniques.name: Symbol
techniques.say: The camera lingers on “His judgment cometh and that right early” on Norton’s wall, so his end feels like judgement.
techniques.what: Something that stands for a bigger idea.

reps.title: The lasting damage of power
reps.say: Released at last, Red still asks permission to go to the toilet: the prison is still in his head.
reps.start: Even after release, the prison's power lingers:
ideas: Even freedom can't undo forty years of control.
Red's story echoes Brooks's, and we fear it will end the same way.
model: Even after release, the prison's power lingers in Red's mind.
Given Brooks's old room and his job bagging groceries, Red still asks his manager for permission to go to the toilet, and admits he thinks about breaking parole just to be sent back.
Darabont deliberately retraces Brooks's steps, so we fear that Red's story will end the same way.
Forty years of control have conditioned him so completely that freedom feels frightening, a sobering reminder that the damage done by abusive power does not end at the prison gate.

reps.title: Honesty as a kind of freedom
reps.say: Red stops performing for the board, calls “rehabilitated” a made-up word, and is finally released.
reps.start: Red finds freedom only when he stops playing the system's game:
ideas: Red is finally freed when he stops performing for the system.
Honesty is the one thing the board can't control.
model: Red finds freedom only when he stops playing the system's game.

At his final hearing, after forty years, he tells the board that 'rehabilitated' is just a made-up word and that he regrets the foolish young man who committed his crime; for the first time he no longer cares what they decide, and he is released.
The hearing is filmed just like the earlier ones, so the repetition draws attention to what has changed: this time, Red is candid.
His sincerity is liberating, suggesting that the one thing the system cannot control is a man who refuses to perform for it.

words: reformed, made fit to live in society
trained to think or act a certain way
details: After forty years, Red tells the board that 'rehabilitated' is a made-up word.
He says he regrets the foolish young man who committed his crime, and he is released.
Outside he gets Brooks's old room and job, and asks his manager for permission to go to the toilet.

techniques.name: Repetition
techniques.say: The hearing is filmed just like Red’s earlier ones, so we notice what has changed: this time he tells the truth.
techniques.what: Repeating a scene or shot so we compare the two.

techniques.name: Parallel
techniques.say: Red is given Brooks’s room and Brooks’s job, and the film retraces Brooks’s steps, so we fear the same ending.
techniques.what: Two characters or stories set side by side, so we compare them.

reps.title: Freedom beyond power's reach
reps.say: Red keeps his promise, breaks parole and finds Andy on a beach, far beyond the reach of any prison.
reps.start: The ending places its characters beyond the reach of power:
ideas: The two men end up where no prison and no warden can reach them.
The open sea is the opposite of the walls of Shawshank.
model: The ending places Red and Andy far beyond the reach of any warden.

Keeping his promise, Red finds Andy's box beneath the rock near Buxton, then carves 'So was Red' beside Brooks's words, breaks parole and heads south to find Andy working on a boat on the beach at Zihuatanejo.
Darabont's final wide shot pulls back over the Pacific until the two men are tiny figures in a boundless blue world, the opposite of Shawshank's grey walls.
The open sea affirms that the prison's power, however brutal, was never total: these men end their story in a place where no one owns them.

reps.title: Hope defeats the system
reps.say: “Hope is a good thing”: the very thing Red once called dangerous is what saves him.
reps.start: Ultimately, hope proves stronger than the system:
ideas: The hope Red once called dangerous is what saves him.
The ending leaves us believing that hope outlasts power.
model: Ultimately, hope proves stronger than the system.

Andy's letter in the box tells Red that hope is a good thing, maybe the best of things, and that no good thing ever dies; the very feeling Red once called dangerous carries him to the beach at Zihuatanejo.
Red's closing voiceover is a string of wishes for the future, so the narration that began in a parole hearing ends on an open shore.
The film's final message is triumphant and uplifting: the abuse of power can crush men's bodies for decades, but it cannot destroy the belief that finally sets them free.

meeting again after a long time apart
the way a story is settled
details: Red finds Andy's box under the rock near Buxton, with money and a letter.
He carves 'So was Red' beside Brooks's words and breaks his parole.
He finds Andy working on an old boat on a sunlit beach in Zihuatanejo.

Yet the film refuses to let power have the last word: Andy beats Norton at his own game.
